body:
Shadow writes:   "I wish I could read a wide-ranging review of what various
people think of the manifesto."
**********************
A wide-ranging review:

	Once upon a time, mankind lived in perfect harmony with nature.  Everything
had passion and meaning and all human needs were provided for by the benevolent
Earth-goddess.  Then the evil scientists came along and forced everyone to buy
things and raped the Earth and now nothing has any meaning and we are all
zombies.  If we destroy everything then we will automatically go back to the
golden age and we'll be back in la-la-land and everything will be great again. 
Don't you just love religious zealots?
		Adam Ierymenko		
		in alt.fan.unabomber					
________________________________
	The genesis for these arguments could go all the way back to the Bible
(Cain/Abel) or Plato (Phaedrus) but are much more common starting about 1740 
or so.  German philosophers, in particular, covered this ground again and again
and again.  Also, in Russia, Tolstoy and Dostoevski extensively covered this
ground.  Dostoevski's Notes from Underground is in fact the autobiography of TK
written 130 years before the fact.  Tolstoy said: "As technology increases,
individual freedom decreases."  Gad, these truths are so old! 
	The manifesto is all over the place: download, read, read some more, and good
luck.
		Ehrlich	
		in alt.fan.unabomber							

________________________________
	What man wants is simply independent choice, whatever that independence may
cost and wherever it may lead.
		Fedor Dostoevski,  Notes from Underground, pt. 1. Ch. 7 (1864)
.________________________________
	Kaczynski dared to say what most people are too afraid, oversocialized, or
blind to say.  He confronted our social problems with a thoughtful analysis
which is rare in a time when media stupidity is the main source of most
people's "information" about the world around them.
		Ricardo Hector Gonzalez
		in alt.fan.unabomber
.________________________________
	Though many important differences emerged as technological pessimism in
Germany changed its political coloration, the impulse to see technology, not
political decision, as the source of modern problems, remained a powerful
current of German thinking and feeling.
		Jeffrey Herf, ���Belated Pessimism: Technology and Twentieth Century German
Conservative Intellectuals,��� in Technology, Pessimism and Post Modernism, ed.
By Yaron Ezrahi et al. (1994)
________________________________
	The Manifesto is just a second-rate regurgitation of other peoples' ideas.
		Hank	
		in alt.fan.unabomber	
[Mignarda's view]			 				
.________________________________
[A response to Mignarda's view]
	Philosophies do not spring full grown into consciousness as Pallas Athena was
born from the head of Zeus.  They suffer a natural and historical, not to say
psychological and sociological, growth; only slowly do they develop to
maturity.  Even in maturity philosophies undergo change and alteration, advance
and decay.
		Carl Mitcham, Thinking Through Technology (1994)		
________________________________
	My fundamental disagreement with the Manifesto is that I don't see
freedom being lost, but rather I see freedom increased.
	John McCarthy, Computer Science Department, Stanford, CA 94305
(one of the founders of Artificial Intelligence) in alt.fan.unabomber
________________________________
	This repeated labeling of the manuscript as "rambling" implies to me
either the people using the word:
	(1) have not actually read the manuscript; or
	(2) they are attempting to not-so-subtly discourage others from reading it, by
labeling it with a word having connotations that put most people off; or
	(3) (far more likely) they prefer not to have to think about subjects that
bring up painful issues about the image we have of ourselves as a society
because they are too glaringly obvious.
		Ward Nicholson	
		in alt.fan.unabomber						
________________________________	[T]hink you have it partly right with
your number one observation.  There probably was someone in the media who
originally read it and like anyone else had his/her opinion, which in this case
was described as "rambling".  The rest of the deadline pressured media pack now
has a nice short description --  so why bother reading it? 
		John R. Capelluto		
		in alt.fan.unabomber			    		
________________________________
	When writing a document as long as the manifesto without the benefit of a word
processor, there are bound to be many disjointed discussions. 
		Andrew Davie	
		in alt.fan.unabomber							
________________________________
	[Y]ou either have to write a long essay, or be content with an 
incomplete and imprecise expression of your opinion.
	Letter from Ted Kaczynski
________________________________
	It is without a doubt constructed of theoretical bric a brac, 
nonetheless it contains some impressive views on the life we consent to 
lead.  Views, the strangeness of which are linked to the extreme asocial 
nature of the life led by their author for more than eighteen years.  But 
views that, though distorted and distorting, make us see what we will 
not admit; for example that "it is impossible to reform the industrial
technological complex," by virtue of the fact that "restriction of freedom is
inevitable in industrial society."
		Annie LeBrun, April 16, 1996 -- Paris, France
Introduction to a French translation of the Unabomber Manifesto
________________________________
	I have to confess I hadn't read the manifesto that well
until recently even though I have swam along with this newsgroup for nearly 2
years.  Now that I have been reading it I am quite startled at the relative
daring he has to any other writer.  Most writers are not so direct.
		John Biosicfix
		in alt.fan.unabomber
________________________________
	Didn't anybody else who read his manifesto think it was more anti
establishment than anti-technology.  I mean, technology was a part of it, but
not nearly as much as the media focused on it.
		Craig Wood
		in alt.fan.unabomber
________________________________
	Not anti-establishment per se, but the establishment's use of technology. 
Nothing he (they) said was simply anti-government, and it was actually stated
several times that it wasn't the government which was found objectionable.  
Just the "system's" use of technology in controlling people.
		D Leif Rustvold		
		in alt.fan.unabomber					
________________________________
	According to his writings, Mr. Kaczynski chronically views 
accidental or intentional personal contact with other people, newspaper 
articles, scientific advances, commercial and residential development, 
air traffic, and radio and television broadcasts as threats to his 
survival.
		Declaration of David V. Foster, M.D. dated November 12, 1997
________________________________
	As for this guy���s style, he was an unbathed bum living in a shack.  I mean,
the man was in the business of killing innocent people.  That is some "style". 
If you want to read someone's work that is impressive logically read Ayn Rand.
		John Galt 		
		in alt.fan.unabomber							
________________________________
	The most selfish of all things is the independent mind that recognizes no
authority higher than its own and no value higher than its judgment of truth.  
                                
		Ayn Rand, Atlas Shrugged (1957) 
________________________________
	It is a silly prejudice of the intellectual that his is the only 
one that counts.
		Letter from Ted Kaczynski
________________________________
	White liberal pussy!
	(The ever articulate)
	Pyro in alt.fan.unabomber
_________________________
	[H]e fails to establish WHY some of the things he regards as "good" or "evil"
for man ARE so, and so, doesn't really establish a framework of morality within
which he may make some of the assertions about man's needs which he makes. 
Furthermore, I found that his reasoning tends to get a bit shaky when he moves
on to the more crucial issues, viz., why his particular advocacy of violent
attack against INDIVIDUAL scientists and businessmen is justifiable, given that
it is LARGE organizations and the technology that they support which are "to
blame" in his Weltanschauung.
		Robert S Kissel	
		in alt.fan.unabomber		
________________________________
	He regards a physical constraint on what a person can accomplish as
a fact of nature to be endured or got around.  The fact that one cannot walk
100 miles in a day for example.  He regards a social constraint -- the fact
that one can't get material goods without working at a job -- as unendurable. 
Most people look upon physical constraints and social constraints as similar. 
Either is to be endured or got around.  Anger at a social constraint is
appropriate only when the constraint is perceived as arbitrary and/or caused by
someone else violating norms.
		John McCarthy		
		in alt.fan.unabomber			
________________________________
	Here is a rule of thumb for the identification of surrogate activities.  Given
a person who devotes much time and energy to the pursuit of goal 
X, ask yourself this: If he had to devote most of his time and energy to 
satisfying his biological needs, and if that effort required him to use his
physical and mental facilities in a varied and interesting way, would he feel
seriously deprived because he did not attain goal X? If the answer is no, then
the person's pursuit of a goal X is a surrogate activity.   
		Industrial Society And Its Future, by ���FC��� (para 39)
________________________________FC's "real" goals are just those goals that
happen to have been hardwired into our nervous and hormonal systems as a result
of a long series of evolutionary accidents (but then again, FC seems to worship
pure random Chance -- which he sometimes calls Nature -- as a god),  and FC's
"surrogate" goals are those that individuals choose for themselves, rather than
have imposed on them by the brute fact of their genetic heritage.  Which of
these two sets sounds more compatible with human freedom to you?
		Eric Watt Forste 		
		in alt.fan.unabomber				
________________________________
	Does technology cause problems?  Sure.  When man invented the bow and arrow,
game became so easy to catch that he suddenly had a lot of time on his hands,
with nothing to divert him except "surrogate activities" such as painting the
walls of his cave.  It must have been awfully stressful!
		Mark Israel		
		in alt.fan.unabomber					
________________________________
	FC/TK is rather unappreciative of art and music.  Creative, non academic
pursuits can certainly be considered surrogate by FC's definition, but I'll be
damned if he'd be able to come up with a good reason to eliminate them.  It's
like a recent poster was saying about Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs.  Food,
water, shelter, love... it's not enough for everyone.  Even if those are there
in spades.
		Erik Haugsjaa	
		in alt.fan.unabomber						
________________________________
	���Art forms that appeal to modern leftist intellectuals tend to focus
on sordidness, defeat and despair, or else they take an orgiastic tone,
throwing off rational control as if there were no hope of accomplishing
anything through rational calculation and all that was left was to  immerse
oneself in the sensations of the moment.���
		Charles Eicher					
		in rec.arts.fine quoting Industrial Society And Its Future, by 	
���FC��� (para. 17)
________________________________
	I can hear the choir and I can hear the music that infuses the lowest of men
and raises him up to stand as the equal of any god.  But what does that matter?
 Beethoven was just a tool of the system after all.
		Greg Swann				 		
		in rec.arts.prose, alt.prose
________________________________
	Science and technology provide the most important examples of 
surrogate activities.  Some scientists claim that they are motivated by 
"curiosity" or by a desire to benefit humanity.  But it is easy to see that
neither of these can be the principle motive of most scientists.  As for
"curiosity," that notion is simply absurd.  Most scientists work on highly
specialized problems that are not the object of any normal curiosity.   
		Industrial Society And Its Future, by ���FC��� (para. 87)
________________________________
	He has no understanding at all of what motivates scientists.
		Tony Harminc 	
		in alt.fan.unabomber
________________________________	
	Men love to wonder, and that is the seed of science.
		Ralph Waldo Emerson, Society and Solitude (1870)
________________________________
	I think that engineering is what human beings, deep down, want to do.  Not the
only thing, but one of the most basic and satisfying things.  Engineering is an
activity that is fulfilling -- existentially...  To be human is to be
technological.  When we are being technological we are being human.
		Samuel Florman, The Civilized Engineer, (1987)
________________________________
	Our society tends to regard as a "sickness" any mode of thought or 
behavior that is inconvenient for the system, and this is plausible  because
when an individual doesn't fit into the system it causes pain to 
the individual as well as problems for the system.  Thus the manipulation 
of an individual to adjust him to the system is seen as a "cure" for a
"sickness" and therefore as good.   
		Industrial Society And Its Future, by ���FC��� (para. 155)

	Education is no longer a simple affair of paddling a kid's behind when he
doesn't know his lessons and patting him on the head when he does know them. 
It is becoming a scientific technique for controlling the child's development. 

		Industrial Society And Its Future, by ���FC��� (para. 148)
________________________________
	This is one endorsement we didn���t need.
	 	Sylvan Learning Center President Douglas L. Becker
________________________________
	This means that -- despite all the pretentious talk about the aims of
education -- it is not the child in and for himself who is being educated, but
the child in and for the society.  And the society, moreover, is not the ideal
one, with full justice and truth, but society as it is.
		Jacques Ellul, The Technological Society, (1954, tr. 1964)

	Indeed.  If TK is the Unabomber, then the manifesto pretty much amounts to:

         behavior.  *** (para. 115)���

 	���Need more technical personnel? A chorus of voices exhorts kids       
to study science. ***  (para. 119)���
surrounded by 29,000 words of rationalization for his murderous response

		in alt.fan.unabomber

	From reading the first part of his manifesto, I see sincere concern for
society, not personal hatred.
		Tom Robertson 		
		in alt.fan.unabomber						
________________________________
	I would like to ask the guy ... if he believes in making changes for 
the good, why would he be hurting people?  That's the only thing I'd like 
to know. 
		Diogenes Angelakos, the victim of a 1982 bombing 
________________________________
	Where does this strength of emotion for "things" and "ideas" come from?  Why
not people instead?  There is no way one can claim to care about humanity, and
not "be" with people on a regular basis.  Is there?  I think not.  He's a
misanthrope.  That's for sure.
		Erik Haugsjaa		
		in alt.fan.unabomber	
________________________________	
	I see a sort of concern for humanity in the abstract, a concern that humans
will be coerced, controlled, "domesticated", made into a "manufactured
product."  Don't a lot of us share such a concern?  Are we not concerned by
stories of cloning and Deep Blue computers that can outthink a chess genius? 
Are we not repulsed by a future in which our emotions can be packaged on a
chip, or in which our descendants can have their personality customized the way
we would order a customized suit? 
		Shadow	
		in alt.fan.unabomber

	The British mathematician, Alan Turing, [who] he established many of the
theoretical foundations for the computer in the 1930s and 40s... 
took his life by painting an apple with cyanide and biting into it, and 
it makes me think of the forbidden fruit of the tree of knowledge...   We have
work, agriculture, misery and technology out of that.  And I also wonder, in
passing, about Apple computers. 
		John Zerzan, in ���Against Technology��� a talk at Stanford University on April
23, 1997
________________________________
	[The manifesto] so struck a nerve within me that for months I refused to learn
anything about Theodore Kaczynski.  I did not want to connect those words and
ideas to a man out of fear of disappointment. I didn't believe that any man
could live up to the simplistic genius of what I had read, short of Thoreau
himself. 
	Now, two years later, I am surprised, and incredibly proud, to be able to
admit that not once, through any statement, action or reaction, did he 
depart from the demanding ideal that I had set so long ago.
 		Jeff Wilson
		on Unapack webpage

Dr. Tyler: 
***
	Do you think we are likely to be right, in a general way, about the kind of
future that technology is creating for the human race?  If you think we are
wrong, then why do you think so? How would you answer our arguments?  Can you
sketch a PLAUSIBLE scenario for a future technological society that does not
have the negative characteristics indicated by our scenario?  If you think we
are likely to be right about the future, do you consider that kind of future
acceptable? If not, then what, if anything, do you think can be done about it? 
Do you think our analysis of PRESENT social problems is approximately correct?
If not, why not? How would you answer our arguments? If you think we have
identified some present social problems correctly, do you think anything can be
done about them? Will they get better or worse with continued growth and
progress? 
...
FC 
________________________________		 	People quit jobs in
corporations to start their own small businesses, people move from large cities
to the country, people voluntarily conserve water, recycle their trash, and
lower their use of electricity and natural gas.  It seems to me that the
revolution you advocate is already occurring....  [A] ���revolution��� that changes
the economic and technological basis of our society need not be violent or
sudden. 
		Response by UC Berkeley Professor Tom Tyler to ���FC���
________________________________
	Coming from the mouth of a murderer, all of TK's sound reasoning would simply
paint the killer and the political statement with the same evil brush. That's
not fair to citizens who have used peaceful means through the years to improve
society and protect the natural environment. 
The air is cleaner, the water is cleaner, and industries are competing 
for the "green" buyer now more than ever.  Progress is painfully slow, 
but it is true and with the support of the governed.  TK could have been 
a part of the change but instead became like any other serial killer 
who's message will now, in the minds of many, be simply an extension of 
his murderous lunacy. 
		Sshebert
		in newyorktimes.com forum
________________________________
	He himself voided the message when he started sending bombs.  He thought he
was making people listen to him. Instead, he was giving them an excuse not to
listen to him.  He went from prophet to heretic and we lost out, too. 
		Karen 
		in newyorktimes.com forum
________________________________
	We need neither condemn nor condone violence.  When blacks rallied 
around murderer O.J. they struck a media-made gong and gave voice to 
their outrage at the police and justice system. It was not mistaken for 
an endorsement of homicide. 
		Lydia Eccles
		on Unapack webpage
________________________________
	We don't have anything to lose if the Unabomber's actions demonize us and
other anti-establishment groups in the eyes of the public, because we simply
weren't in the eyes of the public before.
		CrimethInc. Workers Bulletin
		on Unapack webpage
________________________________
	I hear veterans like Chomsky, Zinn, Dellinger near hopelessness as they
contemplate a resistance in fragments, thirty years in forced retreat, while a
consciousness-razing, ever-tightening media net systematically deprives us of
any unifying focal point for resistance.
���������������There will not be another Vietnam. The state learned from that.  Did 
we? ...���Dare to be perky!
		Letter from Lydia Eccles (Unapack) to Fifth Estate, published Summer 1997 (in
response to anti-Unabomber article by T. Fulano aka D. Watson)

	What does the Unabomber ask for?  Simple: ���With regard to revolutionary
strategy, the only points on which we absolutely insist are that the single
overriding goal must be the elimination of modern technology?���
	Let���s be real, here, folks.  He knows that ain���t gonna happen.  Anyone this
clearly intelligent who makes such ridiculous demands and has such ridiculous
goals isn���t interested in reforming society.  He���s got a personal ax to grind
based on his own deep problems and inadequacies.
		Unabomber: On The Trail of America���s Most-Wanted Serial 		Killer,
by John Douglas and Mark Olshaker, 113 (1996)
________________________________
	I doubt you will find many people here who want to return to an age of
spear-chucking and rock-hurling.  People here seem much inclined to want what
is termed "appropriate technology."  This could perhaps be either an
agricultural-based economy (similar to Jefferson's ideal), or something with
somewhat non-intrusive high-technology.
		James A. Robinson
		in alt.fan.unabomber
 ________________________________
	If the breakdown is sudden, many people will die, since the world's population
has become so overblown that it cannot even feed itself any longer without
advanced technology.  Even if the breakdown is gradual enough so that reduction
of the population can occur more through lowering of the birth rate than
through elevation of the death rate, the process of de-industrialization
probably will be very chaotic and involve much suffering.   
		Industrial Society And Its Future, by ���FC��� (para. 167)
________________________________
	Dr. Kaczynski's views may have been swept under the rug for now by the very
powers they oppose, but in a hundred years will people have a 
different opinion of him? I think so and I challenge all of you informed
 readers to judge for yourselves by reading the manifesto.   Perhaps you will
see what he meant, and it most definitely is not about killing people. 
It is about where we are going and what the establishment needs to do to 
keep us going there. 
		M Harms
		in CNN forum 
________________________________
	It is an interesting thought that Ted will be viewed differently in the
future.  This will be due, of course, to the freedom of speech and the press
that we all accept as a given. In a totalitarian society his 
writing would be unpublished and he would be snuffed out like a candle, 
never to be heard of or thought of again... 
		John Bruce
		in CNN forum
